info.bio:
Einstürzende Neubauten es una agrupación artísticomusical originado en Berlín que no ha dejado de cambiar desde su comienzo en 1980. Su música se clasifica usualmente como Industrial o experimental, pero estos términos no pueden realmente describir el sonido de la banda.
Una de las características principales de la banda es el uso de instrumentos y sonidos que ellos mismos crearon, acompañados de instrumentos tradicionales. La banda perteneció al movimiento Die Geniale Dilletanten

scenes.name: DAF y el electropunk alemán
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Estudiantes de arte de la pequeña escena de Düsseldorf, rebeldes contra «el imperialismo pop norteamericano»: en Mute, Die Kleinen und die Bösen es electropunk caótico; reducidos al dúo de Gabi Delgado y Robert Görl, en Virgin despojan su música hasta un «brutalismo eurodisco» y son estrellas en Alemania con Alles ist gut y «Der Mussolini». Primitivismo techno, culto al cuerpo, provocación con tabúes nazis y sexuales a lo Genet y Bataille: los verdaderos new romantics, inventores de la electronic body music e influencia en el house de Chicago y el techno de Detroit. Alrededor, Einstürzende Neubauten y Liaisons Dangereuses.

scenes.name: Experimental alemán: Einstürzende Neubauten
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En Alemania, ruido y anarquía más allá del industrial, entre la estética punk y el expresionismo: Der Plan, Die Krupps, P16D4, Die Haut, HNAS y, sobre todo, Einstürzende Neubauten, teatro vivo de la autodestrucción con objetos encontrados y cadencias industriales (Kollaps, Zeichnungen des Patienten OT), más cercanos a Beckett que a Chuck Berry. DAF, Palais Schaumburg y Xmal Deutschland llevan el synth-pop hacia el baile industrial; Malaria, Yello, Die Form (Francia), Maurizio Bianchi (Italia) y Esplendor Geométrico (España).

podcast.title: Early Industrial Pioneers
podcast.body: This German group's initial recordings are described as "wild stuff" within early industrial music, with the aim to showcase that the electric guitar could be used unconventionally or even rendered unnecessary. "Go back and listen to some of their first recordings by groups such as... Germany's Einstein-Dé Noybaden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extreme Sound Experimentation
podcast.body: The group was known for extreme sound experimentation. For example, their singer, Blixa, once had his chest wired with microphones while someone gave him a bearhug until his ribs cracked, and this sound was incorporated into one of their compositions. These extremes became a hallmark of their classroom music. "For example, Blixer, the singer, once wired his chest with microphones and had someone give him a barehug until his ribs cracked, and NoiButton used the sound in one of their compositions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Martin Gore (Depeche Mode)
podcast.body: Martin Gore, the songwriter for Depeche Mode, listed Einstürzende Neubauten among the industrial bands he listened to in his spare time, indicating their significant influence on his musical development and later work with Depeche Mode. "And of course, Einstein's Andy Neubaden. This aggressive approach to music really appealed to Martin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Non-Traditional Instrumentation
podcast.body: In their early days, Einstürzende Neubauten deliberately eschewed conventional instruments, melodies, or chord changes. Instead, they created music using objects like anvils, sledgehammers, broken glass, banging lead pipes, sheet metal, and power tools, aiming to sound like a "15-car pile-up on the floor of a steel plant." "In the beginning, NoiButton didn't even bother with instruments. These guys weren't into chord changes or melodies or anything like that. They made their music with anivals, sledgehammers, by breaking glass and banging-led pipes and sheet metal, and of course, power tools."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift to Chord Changes by Mid-1980s
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, Einstürzende Neubauten had evolved their approach to music, notably beginning to incorporate chord changes into their compositions, marking a departure from their earlier, purely noise-based methodology. "Noe Bowden had discovered to use chord changes, and a new synthesis of styles was developing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Extreme Performance for Sound Recording
xref.body: As the singer for Einstürzende Neubauten, Blixa famously allowed his chest to be wired with microphones and subjected himself to a bearhug that cracked his ribs, with the resulting sounds being incorporated into one of the band's compositions. "For example, Blixer, the singer, once wired his chest with microphones and had someone give him a barehug until his ribs cracked, and NoiButton used the sound in one of their compositions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced by Industrial Bands
xref.body: As the songwriter for Depeche Mode, Martin Gore privately listened to aggressive industrial acts such as Fad Gadget (known for using power drills), Test Department (known for performances in quarries and car factories), and Einstürzende Neubauten. This exposure led him to incorporate industrial elements into Depeche Mode's music as he gained more control. "But if you would ask songwriter Martin Gore, who he listened to in his spare time, he would have listed names like Fad Gadget, the group that liked to use black and decker power drills in their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
